transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-11-20 15:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Jules Moreno (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Northforge Head of ML), David Cho (Infra), Priya Nair (SRE), Marco Silva (Product)

Summary (auto): quick triage of last week's bench run; discrepancy on 99th pct tail vs baseline; discussed KV cache hits, batching, and quantization tradeoffs; agreed to provide raw logs and schedule head-to-head lab run.

Transcript:
[00:00] Samir: hey everyone thanks for jumping on, uh 42 minutes on the calendar, we want to go over the numbers from last week's bench, call out the weird tail and propose next steps. Lena, you wanted to start with context?
[00:18] Lena: yeah thanks Samir, quick context — our primary constraint is 90ms p95 for interactive agent flows, baseline vendor is meeting that in prod but unit cost is high, so we're trying to see if Redwood can hit similar latency at lower token cost. we ran two configs, hosted default and a quantized pipeline on dedicated slot.
[00:38] Jules: just to be clear — the config names in our spreadsheet are "hosted-v2" and "ded-qp4" — I think there was a small mapping mismatch earlier with your labels, that might explain some diffs.
[00:52] David: yeah we accidentally labeled the ded run as ded-q3 in our notes, so indexes didn't line up.
[00:58] Samir: ok, noted. so the cleaned CSV Jules sent later this morning is the source of truth.
[01:08] [01:05] Marco: quick non-tech q, when you say dedicated slot what does that actually map to for us? like GPU type?
[01:15] Jules: it's an A10x-like pool in our lab but for production it's a dedicated gpt-optimized instance set — sorry, kernel selection differs per model. sometimes the transcript here says A10, sometimes A100, it's a bit fuzzy in our notes.
[01:28] Lena: got it. let's run through the numbers then.
[01:31] [02:00] Jules: ok, topline — p50s across the two configs were comparable: hosted-v2 ~28ms p50 on your short-turn prompts, ded-qp4 ~32ms p50. The real divergence is tail: baseline vendor p99 ~78ms, Redwood ded-qp4 p99 ~124ms, and hosted p99 ~160ms. The throughput numbers: baseline sustained 260 reqs/min in our load profile, ded-qp4 sustained 420 reqs/min, hosted peaked at 480 but with higher variance.
[02:45] Priya: whoa — so our throughput looks better on Redwood but tail latency is worse, which is the opposite of our expectation.
[02:53] Jules: yeah, that was surprising to us too. we dug into KV cache hit rates — baseline had a 47% prefix cache hit, our ded run recorded ~12% because the traffic sample had more long-tail prompts and different tokenization.
[03:10] David: that tokenization point is interesting — baseline is using some prompt prefixing that we add at the product layer, maybe their client reuses more prefixes. we can try to align that.
[03:18] Samir: right, so a few immediate suspects: misaligned traffic (prefix distribution), different batching windows, and quantization-induced variability on tail tokens.
[03:29] [04:00] Jules: on batching, Redwood runtime uses continuous batching with a dynamic window tuned to hit latency SLOs; during the run we saw windows expand to 11-14ms under bursts which helps throughput but can increase p99 under heavy tail. if you force smaller windows you lose throughput. it's a tradeoff.
[04:46] Marco: can you show the math: how reducing window affects throughput?
[04:52] Jules: yes, I can attach the sample curve — basically 50% smaller window reduced p99 by ~25ms in lab but throughput dropped 22%.
[05:05] Lena: for us the priority is p95/p99 over raw throughput; cost matters but we can't sacrifice SLAs.
[05:14] Samir: understood. two paths: tune for lower tail (smaller batch windows + more aggressive KV caching) or accept higher tail and use routing fallback to baseline for mission-critical low-latency requests.
[05:28] [06:00] Priya: what's the KV cache tuning knob look like? and is that customer-controlled?
[06:05] Jules: you can configure prefix TTL and cache key sharding on Private and Dedicated; Hosted has sensible defaults but we can enable a "sticky prefix" mode for your top 500 prefixes to increase hit rate. it's not magic — it's about aligning prefix sets.
[06:21] David: fine, we'll extract the top prefixes. Lena: we'll share top 500 prompts.
[06:27] Samir: great. next item — quantization. ded-qp4 used 4-bit quantization to save cost. we saw occasional spikes where attention kernel fallback occurred and that added 30-40ms for some sequences. Jules, can you explain?
[06:44] Jules: sure — certain token sequences trigger kernel codepaths that aren't yet fully optimized in 4-bit mode, leading to serial exec for that chunk. it's rare but correlated with longer prompts. our compiler team has a patch in staging that reduces those fallbacks; we can push it to the ded image for the next run.
[07:02] Lena: how confident are you that patch will reduce p99?
[07:06] Jules: preliminary runs show p99 down by ~18ms for our sample workload. not a silver bullet but helpful.
[07:12] [08:00] Marco: any differences in network overhead vs baseline? maybe their edge is closer to our users.
[08:08] Samir: baseline does use a regional edge that Northforge is colocated with; our hosted endpoints were in a different region for the run which added 8-12ms egress. for the ded runs in our lab network egress was negligible.
[08:24] Priya: ok so compounding factors: region, KV cache hit, batching windows, and quantization fallbacks.
[08:31] Jules: yes. also we saw some GC-like stalls in the client side — the product library triggered a synchronous flush on long sequences. David, did you see that in the client logs?
[08:42] David: right — there was a synchronous flush we added that wasn't in baseline tests; that'll inflate tail. we'll disable it for next head-to-head.
[08:48] [09:00] Samir: excellent. I want to call out one figure — ded sustained throughput ~420 rps/minute against baseline 260 in your profile, so Redwood gives more throughput but tail needs tuning. that's a place we can win on cost per successful request if we tighten tail.
[09:18] Lena: can you clarify cost math? our baseline pricing includes a high per-token fee but better p99. what does cost per request look like after quantization?
[09:26] Jules: in rough terms, quantized ded reduced per-request token compute by ~42% in the run, translating to ~35% predicted cost reduction once you amortize reserved capacity. Hosted delta is smaller. I'll put the cost ladder in the doc.
[09:39] [10:00] Marco: any security/compliance blockers if we move dedicated? we need SOC2 and KMS integration.
[10:08] Samir: Dedicated supports KMS and customer-managed keys for payload encryption at rest and in flight we integrate with your KMS using an envelope key. SOC2 docs we can share — I'll attach in the next email.
[10:18] Lena: do you have audit logs for inference requests? we need per-request traces.
[10:23] Jules: yes, Redwood Console has per-request tracing and you can emit logs to your S3/Kinesis. there's a small retention cost for high volume.
[10:30] Priya: ok good.
[10:33] [11:00] Samir: let's talk proposed lab play: we want to run an aligned head-to-head where we: 1) use identical traffic sample you provide; 2) align prefix sets and tokenization; 3) run baseline and Redwood ded in the same region; 4) enable the compiler patch and sticky-prefix mode. target is one 6-hour run next Thurs. sound good?
[11:54] Lena: yes, that timeline works. we'll share the sample by Friday.
[12:02] David: small ask — can Redwood SE have temporary read-only access to the baseline run logs for correlation? we can masked PII.
[12:10] Jules: we prefer customers to upload masked logs to our secure bucket, but if you can generate redacted archives that's fine. we'll consume them in our lab.
[12:19] [13:00] Marco: also curious about fallback routing — how quickly can you route traffic back to baseline if p99 spikes in prod?
[13:09] Samir: our smart routing supports policy-based fallback. you can set a p99 threshold and traffic above it will route to a fallback pool — baseline could be the fallback. switching is sub-second for new requests; existing in-flight ones will finish on the original path.
[13:22] Priya: any rate limit implications when fallbacking? we don't want to overload baseline.
[13:27] Jules: you set capacity carveouts and circuit-breakers. we can coordinate a handover plan with your SRE to avoid thundering herd.
[13:37] [14:00] Lena: ok let's capture the specific tuning experiments for next run: A) enable sticky-prefix top500; B) reduce batching window by 40% for interactive flow; C) deploy compiler 4-bit patch; D) align region to baseline; E) client flush disabled. any others?
[14:22] Jules: also run ded with a hybrid quantization profile (4-bit for MLP, 8-bit for attention) — might smooth kernel fallbacks.
[14:31] Samir: good one. I'll add hybrid quantization as experiment F.
[14:36] [15:00] David: timeline question — when can we expect the patched image in your lab?
[15:06] Jules: if we get logs today we'll push a canary tomorrow and schedule the lab run Thursday — so you should see patched ded image by Wednesday evening.
[15:14] Lena: perfect. next, on cost tradeoffs, can you provide a banded estimate for dedicated commit vs on-demand hosted?
[15:22] Jules: yes — for your sustained qps, a 3-month reserved commit reduces unit cost by ~28% vs on-demand. I'll include a 1/3/6/12 month ladder in the cost doc.
[15:34] Marco: will that ladder include preemption risk? we need guaranteed capacity for peak.
[15:39] Samir: reserved capacity for Dedicated is SLA-backed; on-demand hosted can be bursty. we'll surface the difference.
[15:45] [16:00] Priya: small implementation item — can you give us a sample Terraform snippet for dedicated slot provisioning and RBAC?
[16:12] Samir: yes I'll share a starter Terraform and an IAM snippet that maps to SRE roles.
[16:18] Jules: also we'll throw in a debug guide for diagnosing kernel fallbacks and cache metrics.
[16:24] [17:00] Marco: are there any features in roadmap that materially change metrics soon? like better kernel fusion or improved batching heuristics?
[17:10] Jules: our next runtime release includes kernel fusion for attention ops and an adaptive batching heuristic that reduces tail by anticipating long sequences. ETA early December. it should help p99 by ~10-15ms in similar workloads.
[17:24] Lena: excellent, that may close the gap.
[17:29] [18:00] Samir: ok recap — action items: Samir to send perf CSV and SOC2/KMS docs; Jules to prepare ded sizing/cost ladder, push canary, and attach debug guide; Northforge to share traffic sample, prefixes, and redacted baseline logs. schedule lab head-to-head Thursday 6-hour window.
[18:38] David: agreed.
[18:41] Priya: quick note — please include instructions for masking user identifiers.
[18:46] Jules: will do.
[18:49] [19:00] Marco: last question, any blockers from legal for sharing logs? we have an NDA in place, right?
[19:06] Samir: yes NDA in place, if you need a one-off DPA for logs we'll coordinate legal next week.
[19:12] Lena: ok thanks everyone, that was productive.
[19:15] Samir: thanks all, we'll follow up with the notes and attachments.
[19:20] (call ends)
